rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate all 10 compounds and identify poorly resolved pairs while minimizing early breakthrough and late retention. The retention window will guide narrower, faster gradients, with temperature available to adjust selectivity.

Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the unresolved pair responds to slope while using the available margin below 10 minutes. This should improve separation if the pair has sufficiently different solvent-strength sensitivities.

The limiting pair improved with a shallower gradient. Narrowing the window further reduces the slope, while the higher starting organic fraction should help keep the last peak below 10 minutes; retain 40 C to isolate these gradient effects.

Narrow the gradient window another step to push the limiting pair above R = 1.5. Raising phi0 alongside lowering phi1 should offset much of the added retention, keeping the last peak near 9.6 minutes while preserving early-peak separation.
Injection 4 reached the maximum CRF. Increase only temperature to test whether the run can be shortened while retaining full resolution, keeping injection 4 as the proven optimum-score fallback.

Test whether a larger temperature increase carries the limiting pair through an elution-order reversal and restores separation in a shorter run. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate temperature selectivity, with injection 4 retained as the maximum-score fallback.

Slightly flatten the gradient at 55 C to try to raise the new limiting pair from R = 1.41 above 1.5. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially matching the maximum CRF with a shorter separation than injection 4.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten the separation while retaining the successful temperature and endpoint from injection 7. The resulting shallower gradient may preserve the critical separations; monitor the early peaks for compression.

Lower phi0 to recover the selectivity and early-peak retention lost in injection 8, while shortening the gradient to target a faster separation. This tests whether the improved starting conditions can preserve both critical pairs under a steeper gradient.

Test a modestly steeper gradient to shorten the fully resolved 8-minute separation from injection 9. Lowering phi0 may help preserve the critical middle-pair selectivity while the higher endpoint accelerates late elution.

The 55 C methods are approaching a resolution limit, so test a substantially cooler selectivity regime with a faster gradient. This may separate the critical cluster through elution-order changes while keeping late retention below 10 minutes; the maximum-score methods remain available.

Test the upper temperature limit with a faster gradient to seek a fully resolved separation shorter than 8 minutes. Higher temperature may improve the previously limiting pair, but the neighboring cluster must be checked for new co-elutions or order reversals.

Raise phi0 at 60 C to test whether the nearly co-eluting middle pair separates after an order reversal, as its selectivity was sensitive to phi0 in earlier runs. This also targets a shorter separation, while the early peaks should retain more separation than at phi0 = 0.20.

Test a steeper gradient on the apparent order-reversed branch at 60 C, where it may improve rather than compress the limiting pair. Changing only tG will reveal this slope response while targeting a substantially shorter separation.

Return to the fully resolved conditions of injection 9 and increase only phi1 by one grid step. This tests a modest speed improvement while avoiding the competing unresolved pairs encountered at 60 C.

Use a gradient slope between injections 9 and 15, targeting full resolution with the last peak around 7.8 minutes. The lower endpoint remains above the observed elution window, so all peaks should still elute during the gradient.

Increase only phi1 from injection 10 to test a faster gradient at the lower starting organic fraction. The extra separation of its middle pair may accommodate the steeper slope, but the marginal R = 1.50 pair requires checking.

Increase the gradient slope slightly from injection 17 to test the speed limit of this fully resolved selectivity regime. The last peak should elute sooner, although the middle pair at R = 1.59 may fall below full resolution.

Explore a faster version of the maximum-score 40 C method using a higher starting fraction and a slightly shallower slope. This tests whether the critical middle pair remains resolved while the early peaks retain sufficient separation.

Trim injection 17 to the same initial composition and gradient slope but a shorter programmed gradient, ending above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction of 0.57. This should preserve its maximum CRF and 7.60-minute separation while eliminating unused gradient time.

Test an intermediate cooler selectivity regime with a fast gradient, seeking full resolution below the current 7.60-minute benchmark. The 25 C and 40 C results suggest substantial movement within the middle cluster, so 35 C may offer a useful separation window.

Test the unexplored 50 C regime with a steep gradient to seek a faster, order-reversed separation of the critical cluster. This is exploratory; injection 20 remains the proven maximum-score method with a 7.60-minute last peak.

Preserve injection 9’s successful starting composition and slope while trimming the unused gradient endpoint. This should retain its maximum CRF and approximately 8-minute last peak, with a larger resolution margin than injection 20.

Test a shallower version of injection 7 to increase the minimum-resolution margin while targeting a last peak just below 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already established; this run seeks a less marginal fully resolved alternative.

Use a slope between injections 7 and 24 to target full resolution with more margin than the fastest method and a last peak around 9.3 minutes. This final run tests a shorter alternative to injection 24 while retaining its favorable temperature and starting composition.
